research_notes: Research was done on 2026-10-10 with a web search tool. The container's network policy blocked direct page fetches from nasa.gov, arxiv.org and most other hosts, so every source below was checked through search-result summaries of that page, not by reading the full text. Treat 'verified' as 'consistent across the summaries of the cited primary/standard sources'. Before publishing, a human should open S01, S02, S04 and S06 directly.
assumptions: The Moon disappears instantly and completely at t = 0: its mass, gravity and reflected light all vanish. No debris, no impact.
This is physically impossible (mass-energy cannot simply vanish); it is a thought experiment used to isolate what the Moon does for Earth.
Everything else in the Solar System continues unchanged.
Long-term results for Earth's tilt come from numerical models of a moonless Earth; they are not observations.

claims.text: An object cannot simply vanish; deleting the Moon breaks conservation of mass-energy, so the scenario is a thought experiment.
claims.notes: Basic physics; stated as the premise's limit.

claims.text: The Earth–Moon barycenter lies on average about 4,671 km from Earth's center — inside Earth, roughly 1,700 km below the surface.
claims.notes: Consistent across Wikipedia barycenter and Orbit of the Moon articles. Script rounds to ~4,700 km.

claims.text: Earth is about 81 times more massive than the Moon.
claims.notes: Stated by secondary sources in search results; standard value.

claims.text: Earth's mean orbital velocity around the Sun is 29.78 km/s.
Earth moves around the Earth–Moon barycenter at roughly 12 m/s.
claims.notes: Calculation: 2π × 4,671 km / 27.32 days (sidereal month) ≈ 12.4 m/s. NASA sheet gives the period as 27.3 d; the 27.32 d value was not checked against NASA directly.

claims.text: Removing the Moon would not knock Earth out of its orbit; Earth's path around the Sun would change only slightly.
claims.notes: Follows from C03/C04: a 12 m/s change against 29,780 m/s is ~0.04%.

claims.text: A full Moon on a clear night gives about 0.05–0.3 lux; ~0.25 lux is a typical single value.
claims.notes: S17 measured 0.26 lux during an exceptionally bright 2016 supermoon.

claims.text: A clear moonless sky (starlight plus airglow) gives about 0.002 lux.
claims.notes: Standard order-of-magnitude reference value; some measurements are lower (0.0006–0.0009 lux). Script says 'around a hundredth' (0.002/0.25 ≈ 1/125), which is conservative.

claims.text: Nocturnal dung beetles orient using polarized moonlight, and on moonless nights can use the Milky Way.
claims.notes: Lund University and Wits research.

claims.text: Many reef corals time mass spawning to the lunar cycle; the light-sensitive cry2 gene in Acropora corals is most active on full-moon nights and is linked to spawning timing. Temperature, tides and day length are also cues.
claims.notes: Press release of Levy et al. 2007 (Science); primary paper not opened.

claims.text: Without moonlight cues, coral spawning could become less synchronized, lowering fertilization success; how severe this would be is unknown.
claims.notes: Reasoned from C09; open question.

claims.text: The Sun's tide-generating force is about 46% of the Moon's (NOAA: about half).
With only the Sun, tidal forcing would be roughly a third of today's typical combined forcing.
claims.notes: 0.46 / (1 + 0.46) ≈ 0.32. Real local tides depend on basin resonance, so 'roughly a third' is a global rule of thumb, not a prediction for any specific coast.

claims.text: Spring and neap tides come from the changing alignment of the Sun and Moon.
Sun-only tides would follow a solar rhythm, so high water would arrive at nearly the same clock time each day.
claims.notes: The solar semidiurnal constituent has a period of exactly 12 hours, unlike the lunar 12 h 25 min.

claims.text: Removing the lunar tidal bulge would not cause a giant wave; open-ocean equilibrium tidal heights are well under a meter, so the sea would readjust over hours like an ordinary falling tide.
claims.notes: Equilibrium lunar amplitude is of order 0.5 m; reasoning, not a modeled result.

claims.text: Weaker tides would narrow intertidal zones, reducing habitat for species adapted to them.
claims.notes: Qualitative reasoning.

claims.text: Total solar eclipses on Earth are caused only by the Moon; without it there would be none.
claims.notes: Definitional.

claims.text: Lunar laser ranging shows the Moon receding by about 3.8 cm per year.
Tidal friction slows Earth's rotation, lengthening the day by roughly 2 milliseconds per century (published estimates range ~1.7–2.5 ms).
claims.notes: Sources disagree on the exact value; script says 'roughly two milliseconds'.

claims.text: Without the Moon most tidal braking stops, so Earth's day would lengthen far more slowly over geological time.
claims.notes: Solar tides would still brake a little.

claims.text: Earth's axial tilt is about 23.4°, and over tens of thousands of years it varies only between about 22.1° and 24.5°. The tilt causes the seasons.
claims.notes: Laskar 1993: ~1.3° variation around a 23.3° mean.

claims.text: The Moon is responsible for about two-thirds of luni-solar precession (~50.3 arcseconds per year in total).
Laskar, Joutel & Robutel (1993) found Earth currently avoids a chaotic zone thanks to the Moon; without the Moon, the chaotic zone for the obliquity would extend from near 0° to about 85°.
claims.notes: This is a statement about a published model result. Li & Batygin 2014 also find chaos in 0–85° for a moonless Earth.

claims.text: Lissauer, Barnes & Chambers (Icarus, 2011) integrated moonless-Earth spin directly and found much more limited obliquity variations — reported as roughly 10–20° over hundreds of millions of years.
claims.notes: Range figure comes from press coverage; NASA abstract says no typical integration reached more than 65% of the range allowed by frequency-map analysis.

claims.text: A swing of 10–20° in obliquity would substantially change the distribution of sunlight and therefore climate zones, ice-sheet growth and monsoons.
claims.notes: Laskar calls the Moon a potential climate regulator; specifics are reasoning.

claims.text: Obliquity changes of this kind unfold over tens of thousands to millions of years.
Specific time (9:41 p.m.), city setting, and the 'lamp / clock / steering wheel' metaphor.
claims.notes: Creative framing, not a factual claim.

open_questions: How chaotic would a moonless Earth's tilt really be? Laskar (1993) vs Lissauer et al. (2011) differ; Li & Batygin (2014) add nuance.
How much would loss of moonlight cues reduce coral spawning success?
The exact modern rate of day lengthening (1.7 vs ~2.3–2.5 ms per century) depends on method and time window.
